entries.clue: Cause agitation, removing central piece of footrest (4,2)

indicatorNotes.removing: Removing says a named piece leaves the word that follows, so what is wanted is the letters still standing once it has gone.
indicatorNotes.central piece: The central piece of a word of seven letters is the single one in the middle, with three on either side of it.

blocks.note: the metal loop hanging from a saddle that carries a rider's foot
the fourth of those seven letters, the one the removal takes out

annotation.surface: Making a fuss by pulling the middle section out of a piece of furniture.
annotation.walkthrough: A footrest in a crossword is the rider's loop rather than the stool by the fire, and its centre is one letter, not a slab of wood. The enumeration (4,2) is the other tell: one word goes in and two come out.
annotation.definitionFit: To stir up a crowd or stir up trouble is to work something into agitation, the deliberate raising of a fuss.

blocks.note: the vehicles moving along a road, counted together as one flow
dealing in goods, and especially dealing in the goods nobody admits to — arms, drugs, people

annotation.surface: The business of moving goods from one place to another.
annotation.walkthrough: Two bare nouns with nothing joining them is the shape a double definition always takes, and here they are the traffic a commuter sits in and the traffic customs seizes. The second sense is mostly a verb now: to traffic in something.
annotation.definitionFit: Traffic is the flow of vehicles on a road, and it is also trade in something — the arms traffic, to traffic in stolen goods.

indicatorNotes.announced: Something announced is said out loud, so the word in front of it is wanted for its noise and not for its spelling.

blocks.note: entitlements are rights — human rights, the right to silence — and that word said aloud can be written another way

annotation.surface: Someone reading out the entitlements that come with a church service.
annotation.walkthrough: English gives this one sound three spellings — rights, rites, writes — and only the crossing letters say which the grid wants. 'For' contributes nothing but the join between sound and meaning.
annotation.definitionFit: Rites are the fixed forms a religion performs — the last rites, a burial rite — so religious ceremonies names them straight.

blocks.note: the sharp preserve spooned out beside cold meat and cheese
the fix somebody has got themselves into — they are in a right one

annotation.surface: An instruction to enjoy being in trouble.
annotation.walkthrough: Read as a sentence the clue tells you to savour your difficulties; read as a crossword it is two nouns set side by side. The food sense is British — a jar of sharp chopped preserve eaten with cheese — and the idiom about being in one is older than the jar.
annotation.definitionFit: A pickle is the sharp preserve served as a relish with cold meat, and to be in a pickle is to be in an awkward spot.

entries.clue: The majority of Half Moon Street (4)

indicatorNotes.Half: Half of the word beside it is all that is wanted; the clue does not say which half, and only the front one joins on to what follows.

blocks.note: half of its four letters, cut at the halfway mark and taken from the front
st. is how a street is written on an envelope

annotation.surface: The greater part of a London address.
annotation.walkthrough: Half Moon Street is a real Mayfair address, which is what makes the capital letters look innocent. The setter wants the three words taken one at a time instead.
annotation.definitionFit: Most is the greater part of a thing — most of the cake, most of the street — which is what the majority means.

entries.clue: Be prone to additional exterior for dramatist (7)

indicatorNotes.exterior: What is on the exterior is on the outside, so the word named beside it opens up and wraps round the piece already in hand.

blocks.note: anything additional is more
to be prone is to lie flat, face down

annotation.surface: Somebody inclined to put an extra layer on the outside.
annotation.walkthrough: Molière was the stage name of Jean-Baptiste Poquelin, the French comic playwright of Tartuffe and The Misanthrope, and grids drop his accent. 'Be prone to' reads as an inclination and means lying down.
annotation.definitionFit: Molière wrote comedies for the seventeenth-century French stage, so the bare word dramatist names him by his trade — a definition by example.

indicatorNotes.destroyed: Something destroyed has been knocked apart, and letters knocked apart go back together in another order.

blocks.note: five letters across two words, every one of them used

annotation.surface: An animal ruined by somebody's nastiness.
annotation.walkthrough: The pet is the trap: the sentence asks you to picture a creature coming to harm, and the setter only wants its five letters. Little words like 'is' are the setters' favourite place to hide half an anagram.
annotation.definitionFit: Spite is the small deliberate nastiness done to hurt somebody, which is what malice names.

entries.clue: Small party with artist, a sign of autumn (5)

blocks.note: Lib is the short form of Liberal, one of Britain's smaller parties — the Lib Dems get the same treatment
RA stands for Royal Academician, the crossword's standing artist

annotation.surface: A modest gathering with a painter present.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Small party' is the political kind, not a quiet evening in with six friends. The zodiac sign runs from late September, which is what lets autumn stand in for a set of dates.
annotation.definitionFit: The scales cover late September to late October, so naming the season is a fresh way of pointing at one sign of the zodiac.

blocks.note: S is the compass point and the standard short form for southern
the Tate is Britain's national collection of modern and British art, at Millbank in London and again at Bankside

annotation.surface: A gallery somewhere in the south of the country.
annotation.walkthrough: The comma is the only thing separating definition from wordplay, and the line reads perfectly well as a single phrase without it. 'Say' here is the verb, not the 'for example' that setters usually mean by the word.
annotation.definitionFit: To state something is to say it plainly and for the record — state your name — so the two verbs swap directly.

indicatorNotes.stirred: Stirring mixes a thing up, and letters mixed up come out in a different order from the one they went in.

blocks.note: the five letters that get mixed

annotation.surface: A tin of paint being given a stir.
annotation.walkthrough: Paint genuinely is stirred before use, so the instruction disappears into the picture it makes. The same idea is also spelt INEPT, but that word means clumsy rather than ill-suited, and only one of the two fits here.
annotation.definitionFit: Inapt means not apt — a remark that does not suit the moment is an inapt one — so unsuitable is the plain synonym.

entries.clue: Still off after this French musician (7)

indicatorNotes.off: Milk that is off has gone bad, and letters that have gone bad no longer stand in the order they were written.
indicatorNotes.after: After sends the shuffled letters behind the piece named next, so the French word leads and they follow it.

blocks.note: ce is French for this — ce soir, this evening
the same five letters, standing in a new order

annotation.surface: A player who is still absent after an encounter with something French.
annotation.walkthrough: 'This French' is a construction worth learning: the language is named after the English word to be translated, and schoolroom vocabulary is all a daily puzzle ever asks for. 'Off' reads as absent and is the shuffle.
annotation.definitionFit: A cellist is whoever plays the cello, so musician names the player by the job — a definition by example.

indicatorNotes.Awful: Something awful is in a dreadful state, and letters in a dreadful state have fallen out of the order they were written in.

blocks.note: seven letters, every one of them used

annotation.surface: Somebody getting a dreadful telling-off for not doing as they were told.
annotation.walkthrough: An earful is a loud scolding in British usage, which is what makes the plural read as ordinary English. The abstract noun at the end settles the grammar: not refusing, not refused.
annotation.definitionFit: A refusal is the act of saying no to what was asked, which is non-compliance put as a noun.

blocks.note: ere is the old poet's word for before — ere long, ere the sun sets
ct. is the short form printed on a street sign and a case list

annotation.surface: Somebody on their feet in front of a judge.
annotation.walkthrough: The line reads as one phrase about appearing in court, so there is no visible seam between the definition and the wordplay. 'Before' looks like the joinery and is carrying three of the five letters.
annotation.definitionFit: Erect means upright, held on end — a soldier stands erect — so it does the work of standing up.

blocks.note: S is the compass point and the standard short form for southern
the sailors who work a ship are its crew

annotation.surface: Sailors from the south of the country doing a dance.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Twist' is a verb here, what the wrist does to a cap, rather than the dance the sailors suggest. A ship's screw is its propeller, so the answer never actually leaves the water.
annotation.definitionFit: To screw something is to turn it round on its thread, and twist names the same movement of the hand.

entries.clue: Country copper in love, back to front (7)

indicatorNotes.in: In puts the metal named before it inside the word that follows rather than alongside it.
indicatorNotes.back to front: What stood at the back goes to the front, so the last letter of the word named travels round to lead it and the rest shuffle along.

blocks.note: to love is to adore, and the instruction swings that word's final letter round to the head of it
Cu is the symbol for copper in the periodic table

annotation.surface: A rural policeman in love and getting everything the wrong way round.
annotation.walkthrough: Copper is British slang for a policeman, and 'country copper' reads as one phrase — a village bobby — which is precisely the join the setter wants you to make. The words break the other way: the country is the definition and the metal is the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: Ecuador is the South American republic named after the equator running through it, so country names it by its kind.

indicatorNotes.broken: A broken thing has come apart, and letters that have come apart are put back together in another order.

blocks.note: the five letters that come apart

annotation.surface: Bringing in the crops with a snapped-off weapon.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Harvests' is the plural verb — he harvests — and not a row of nouns, so the s at the end belongs to the grammar rather than to a field. Breakage words are the commonest anagram signal in a daily puzzle.
annotation.definitionFit: To reap is to cut and gather a crop, so harvests is the same verb in the same third-person form.

indicatorNotes.sort of: To sort is to arrange, so the word in front is re-sorted into a different arrangement of the same letters.

blocks.note: seven letters, all of them used

annotation.surface: A less fancy kind of chocolate centre.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sort of' reads as a hedge — a sort of chocolate — and is the instruction to re-sort. The stuff itself is caramelised nuts ground to a paste, which is why it turns up inside a shell rather than on its own.
annotation.definitionFit: Praline is the caramelised-nut paste that fills a chocolate shell, so the definition names it by where a solver has met it.

indicatorNotes.sounding: Sounding asks for the noise the words in front make, not the letters they are written with.

blocks.note: somebody more reserved is shyer, and said aloud that word can be spelt another way

annotation.surface: A quieter sort of English county.
annotation.walkthrough: The hyphen glues the sound instruction to the words it works on, so the whole thing reads as one adjective. A shire is the old English county — the ending of Yorkshire and Cheshire — and 'the Shires' still means the rural English midlands.
annotation.definitionFit: A shire is a county in English usage, the word that ends most county names and stands alone for the same thing.

entries.clue: County of Northern Ireland where social worker on edge (6)

indicatorNotes.on: In a down entry what sits on something is above it, so the first piece goes in at the top and the second underneath.

blocks.note: ants live in colonies and labour for the nest, which makes the ant the crossword's social worker
the edge of a cup or a wheel is its rim

annotation.surface: A care professional in Ulster on the point of cracking.
annotation.walkthrough: 'On edge' is the trap: it reads as nerves and is really two separate pieces of wordplay with the joint between them. Antrim is the county along the north-east coast, the one with the Giant's Causeway in it.
annotation.definitionFit: Antrim is one of the six counties of Northern Ireland, facing Scotland across the North Channel.

entries.clue: Not even Sparta yard with Greek spirit (5)

indicatorNotes.Not even: Not even throws away the letters in even positions, leaving the first, third, fifth and so on of what follows.

blocks.note: the two words are read as one run of ten letters and only those in odd positions are kept

annotation.surface: Not even a yard of Spartan ground.
annotation.walkthrough: The instruction runs straight across the gap between the two words, which is what hides it — they have to be treated as one string before any letters are picked. A satyr is the goat-legged follower of Dionysus, half man and half beast.
annotation.definitionFit: A satyr is a woodland spirit of Greek myth, so the definition points at mythology while the surface points at drink.

indicatorNotes.in: In says the letters wanted are sitting inside the words that follow, unbroken and in the order they already stand.

blocks.note: the run starts near the end of the first word and finishes inside the second

annotation.surface: Somebody with faith in a booming sector of the economy.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Growth industry' is a stock phrase, so the eye slides over the join between its two words — and the join is exactly where the letters straddle. 'Believer in' reads as one unit and is the definition plus the instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: A Hindu is an adherent of Hinduism, so believer names the person by the fact of the faith rather than by its content.

entries.clue: In a short time, goes up with English rope (5)

indicatorNotes.goes up: In a down entry what goes up is read from the bottom end, so the phrase in front of it is written in backwards.

blocks.note: what happens in a short time happens soon, and that word is entered the other way about
E is the standard short form for English

annotation.surface: A flag due to go up shortly on a length of English cord.
annotation.walkthrough: The comma is doing real work: it marks where the phrase to be turned round stops. 'Rope' is the definition, and the answer is the running loop tied in one rather than the coil itself.
annotation.definitionFit: A noose is a rope worked into a running loop — the hangman's, or a lasso — so the material names the thing made of it.

entries.clue: Falls back on another occasion with artist (7)

annotation.definitionNote: The waterfall is always spoken of in the plural — the Falls — while the word answering here is the singular name the place goes by, so the number belongs to the place name rather than to the word.

indicatorNotes.back: Something that goes back in an across entry is read from its right-hand end, so the words named are written in reverse.

blocks.note: on another occasion is again, and those letters are taken the other way round
RA stands for Royal Academician, the crossword's standing artist

annotation.surface: Somebody resorting to an old habit once more, in the company of a painter.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Falls back on' is a single idiom about resorting to something, and the setter has cut it into three jobs: definition, reversal instruction and joinery. The cataract itself is on the border between Canada and New York State.
annotation.definitionFit: The river's name is used on its own for the cataract it drops over — a trip to Niagara means the water, not the water course.

indicatorNotes.found in: What is found in something is already sitting inside it, so the letters stand in the words that follow with nothing done to them.

blocks.note: the run begins in the last letters of the first word and carries straight on into the second

annotation.surface: An extra item turning up inside a large charitable gift.
annotation.walkthrough: The enumeration is the most useful thing in the clue: a hyphenated three-and-two narrows the field before the hiding place has been found. 'Found in' is doing its literal job for once, which is rare enough to be worth spotting.
annotation.definitionFit: An add-on is an extra fitted to something already complete — a software add-on, an add-on to a policy — which is what an accessory is.

entries.clue: Put in a fresh demand for instrument minus case, initially (7)

indicatorNotes.minus: Minus takes away whatever is named after it from the word already in hand.
indicatorNotes.initially: Initially asks for the very start of the word beside it — its first letter, and nothing more of it.

blocks.note: the recorder is the plastic pipe handed to every British schoolchild at about the age of seven
the letter that opens the word, taken on its own and then taken away

annotation.surface: Ordering a musical instrument without the case that normally comes with it.
annotation.walkthrough: An instrument does come in a case, which is what lets the deletion pass as shopping. The comma before 'initially' is the only sign that the case is not being removed whole.
annotation.definitionFit: To reorder is to place an order again, what a shop does when stock runs out, so putting in a fresh demand describes the act.

entries.clue: It's not raining outside first-rate milk factory (5)

indicatorNotes.outside: What is outside goes round, so the words before it wrap themselves about the piece named after it.

blocks.note: weather with no rain falling is dry
A1 means first-rate, and a grid writes the figure one as the letter I

annotation.surface: A spell of fine weather over an excellent creamery.
annotation.walkthrough: A1 comes from Lloyd's shipping register, where it was the top rating a hull could be given, and crossword setters spell the 1 as an I so it can join on to other letters. A whole clause here is doing the work of three of them.
annotation.definitionFit: A dairy is where milk is handled and turned into butter and cheese, so the definition names it by what comes out of it.

blocks.note: to carry a load, or to carry the blame — the same verb does both
named by its kind rather than by its species, which is as vague as a definition is allowed to get

annotation.surface: Somebody carrying a creature about.
annotation.walkthrough: Four letters and a three-word clue leave nothing to work with but the double sense, and the vaguer half is second. The verb survives mostly in older phrasing now: bear arms, bear a grudge, bear left at the junction.
annotation.definitionFit: To bear something is to carry it, and a bear is the big forest mammal, so one set of four letters answers both halves of the clue.

blocks.note: what the Royal Mint does — striking currency, put in the past tense
flavoured with the herb that goes with lamb and new potatoes

annotation.surface: Coins struck and then given a flavour.
annotation.walkthrough: Both halves are past participles, which is why a comma is the only join the clue needs. The herb sense is the one the eye skips: minted lamb, minted peas, and in British slang the same word means rich.
annotation.definitionFit: To mint is to strike coin, and minted also means flavoured with mint — minted lamb on a pub menu.
